title: Rotating pig paddocks for soil recovery
subtitle: Planning the move-and-rest cycle that keeps your land productive.
excerpt: Pigs in a fixed area ruin the ground within weeks. Paddock rotation gives each plot time to recover, regrow pasture, and neutralise the heavy nitrogen and worm-egg load left behind. A minimum of three paddocks in rotation is workable; four or more gives better recovery times.
sourceNotes: Andy Case, Outdoor Pig Production (Crowood Press, 2008). AHDB Pork, Outdoor Pig Systems and Soil Management (2021). John Seymour, The Complete Book of Self-Sufficiency (1976), pigs chapter.

glossaryTerms.definition: The compaction and destruction of soil structure caused by livestock hooves and rooting in wet conditions.
The time a paddock is left ungrazed after livestock. For pig paddocks, a minimum of 6 weeks is needed for significant worm-egg die-off.

content.text: Paddock rotation is the practical method for keeping land productive under pigs. Pigs root aggressively and deposit a heavy dung load; without rotation, a patch quickly becomes bare, wet, and wormy. Moving pigs before the land is fully poached and resting the paddock until it recovers is straightforward to plan and transformative for the land.

As a rough guide, four growers or two sows need around 0.2 hectares (half an acre) in total, split into a minimum of three paddocks. Each paddock is grazed for 4 to 6 weeks before the pigs move on, with each rested paddock getting at least 8 to 12 weeks before pigs return. More land means longer rests and better recovery.
More than 50% of the surface is bare earth or churned mud.
Persistent wet areas that do not dry out between rain events.
Worm burden rising on faecal egg counts despite regular worming.

Set up the next paddock with arc housing, water, and temporary electric fencing before moving the pigs. Moving into an already-set-up paddock is far easier than trying to set up while the pigs are in transit.

Lead with a bucket of feed. Pigs that are used to being fed from a bucket will follow willingly. If the move requires crossing a gateway, keep the entrance wide enough that pigs do not feel funnelled.
Close the old paddock gate immediately and leave it rested. Mark the date in your records.

of at least 6 weeks reduces infective worm larvae on the pasture significantly. Twelve weeks in summer (warm, dry conditions speed larval die-off) is better. Avoid returning pigs before the sward has re-established; bare mud does not recover in a short rest.

Harrowing or scarifying a used paddock in dry spring or summer conditions breaks up dung pats, aerates the soil, and exposes larvae to UV. Light rolling after harrowing helps consolidate compacted surface structure. Lime applications of 2.5 tonnes per hectare on very acid land speed grass recovery.

attrs.cue: Paddock not recovering despite 10 weeks rest
attrs.cause: Soil compaction is too deep for grass to re-establish, or soil pH is very low
attrs.fix: Deep scarify or sub-soil with a hired implement. Test soil pH and apply ground limestone if below 6.0. Oversow with a hard-wearing pasture mix.

attrs.cue: Pigs root through the electric fence to re-enter an old paddock
attrs.cause: Fence voltage too low, or pigs are motivated by the smell of familiar rooting ground
attrs.fix: Check fence energiser output at the wire; aim for above 4,000 V under load. Train young pigs to the fence in a small pen before putting them in paddocks.
